forTheMerger.note: The merger's role topic has no holder and refuses rather than queues, so these reach it through this record and the approval body.
forTheMerger.rule: Read the run, not the lane; and read the review's commit_id, not reviewDecision. Every shape below is a way a name misleads where an id does not.
shapes: The default check-runs page is 30 and these commits carry 25 to 39 runs; read per_page=100 --paginate or required names fall off the page and a green head reads as missing.
A superseded run shows completed/cancelled while a later run of the same workflow succeeded; dispatch at 0085e4b45a48 is the worked example.
A push carrying code and handoff together leaves the code commit with no run of its own; the head that merges is the one GitHub judged.
A .legion-only head carrying skip-checks has no check run at all, which is not a missing verdict: the code head is the commit below it. This head is that shape.
pr-title fires on every pull-request edit, so one head carries many of its runs; the newest decides.
While a pull request is CONFLICTING, GitHub computes no merge ref and runs no on: pull_request workflow for any of its activity.

A genuinely failing non-required lane may belong to another issue: dispatch://INFRA-76 is an Inbox test failing across this project, and this change touches no file under packages/dispatch or packages/proof-editor.

gh pr view --json reviewDecision returns APPROVED for a head the reviewer never saw, because this repository does not dismiss stale approvals on push. reviewDecision is a claim about a review, not about a head; only a review's own commit_id carries one. What makes that safe here is Legion's READY check rather than the forge.

forTheRetro.theParentLesson: A derived pin is worth more than a correct constant, and it holds one level up: a value asserted in a review must be re-derived from the file at the head, because a citation inside a subagent's finding is a claim rather than a reading.
forTheRetro.theSharperForm: The architect's, above mine: writing to strengthen an argument rather than to describe a system. Neither of this tree's documentation failures was careless; both made the case better, which is why neither was checked.
forTheRetro.theSystemProperty: Eight of this review's rounds turned on a sentence rather than on code, and every one of those sentences was operator-facing and about a production system no role in this tree can read. A claim about production in operator-facing documentation needs the fence a derived constant gets: it should name what it rests on.
forTheRetro.theStructuralCure: That paragraph was wrong seven times and every correction was locally right, because each round fixed the sentence and left the structure that produced it. What ended it was not a better sentence but reclaim_doc_test.go — two machine-readable lists the renderer is compared against. The lesson is that a hand-maintained list in prose rots silently, and the fix for the seventh correction is a fence rather than an eighth correction.
forTheRetro.theMutationDiscipline: A mutation must be confirmed applied before its result is read. The tester volunteered this after its own near-miss; I repeated the near-miss within ten minutes of reading it, and caught it only because I had. Every mutation I ran afterwards asserts its anchor first, and so do the tester's scripts.
forTheRetro.whatMostChangedOutcomes: Running the thing rather than reading about it. The shared-cache cold-fill race, the unbounded flock, the subshell exit, the read-only delete, the flock-creates-a-regular-file poisoning: not one was visible in the diff. Every one came from rendering the artefact and executing it.
